extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (Math 216 readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and key lemmas about dimension (Krull/height, transcendence degree, Noether normalization, Hartogs, going-down) for finitely generated algebras and finite-type k-schemes, with exercises and geometric guidance. Useful for proving and applying results about codimension, hypersurface intersections, and normality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendence basis / transcendence degree
rubrics_metrics.description: A transcendence basis of a field extension E/F is a set of elements {x_i} algebraically independent over F such that F({x_i}) ∼ E (compositum is algebraic over each). Any two transcendence bases have the same cardinality; this cardinality is the transcendence degree tr. deg. (A finitely generated field extension has finite transcendence degree.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes reminder that 'algebraic' = 'integral' for field extensions; hint to prove uniqueness of cardinality by substituting basis elements one at a time. Related to Algebraic Fact 9.5.16.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension = transcendence degree (Theorem 11.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a finitely generated domain over a field k, then dim Spec A = tr. deg K(A)/k. Hence for an irreducible k-variety X, dim X = tr. deg K(X)/k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: dimension of an irreducible variety can be computed from the generic point and in any nonempty open set; provides a second proof of the Nullstellensatz (Exercise 11.2.B). The proof uses Noether normalization and induction (see §11.2.7). Warning: false without finite type hypotheses (counterexamples noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a rational map (Definition 11.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X --> Y is a dominant rational map of irreducible k-varieties of the same dimension, the degree of the rational map is the degree of the induced field extension K(X)/K(Y). For reducible X, sum the degrees on components; if a rational map of integral affine varieties of same dimension is not dominant, degree is 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree is multiplicative under composition: deg(ρ ∘ π) = deg(ρ)·deg(π). Will be interpreted in terms of counting preimages of general points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noether Normalization Lemma (11.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A is an integral domain, finitely generated over a field k, with tr. deg_k K(A) = n. Then there exist algebraically independent elements x1,...,xn ∈ A such that A is a finite (hence integral) extension of k[x1,...,xn].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric content: given any integral affine k-scheme X there is a surjective finite morphism X → A^n_k where n = trdeg K(X)/k. Surjectivity follows from Lying Over (Exercise 11.1.E). The lemma is proved (Nagata's proof) by induction on the number of generators and by 'jiggling' variables to produce integral dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nagata's proof / 'jiggling' trick for Noether normalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Given A = k[y1,...,ym]/p with m>n, replace generators by zi = yi − y_m^{r_i} for suitably chosen positive integers r_i so that an algebraic relation yields an integral dependence of y_m over k[z1,...,z_{m-1}], producing a finite extension of one fewer generator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: projecting to a random hyperplane (or 'jiggling' coordinates) typically makes the projection finite; caveat when k is finite one must use the nonlinear substitution. The proof picks r_i so powers of y_m appearing are all distinct, giving a leading y_m^N term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension of affine space (dim A^n = n)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the affine n-space A^n_k one can construct a chain of irreducible closed subsets of length n and prove dim A^n = n; this fact is used in the proof of Theorem 11.2.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses induction: reduce to hypersurfaces and apply Theorem 11.2.1 on lower transcendence degree. Example chain of ideals in k[x1,...,xn]: (0) ⊂ (x1) ⊂ (x1,x2) ⊂ ... ⊂ (x1,...,xn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Codimension equals difference of dimensions for irreducible varieties (Theorem 11.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is an irreducible k-variety and Y an irreducible closed subset with generic point η, then dim Y + dim O_{X,η} = dim X. Hence dim Y + codim_X Y = dim X, so the inequality dim Y + codim_X Y ≥ dim X is actually an equality for irreducible varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to affine case and uses Noether normalization and the Going-Down Theorem for finite extensions of integrally closed domains (Theorem 11.2.12). Exercises 11.2.G–H break the proof into steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Going-Down Theorem for finite extensions of integrally closed domains (11.2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose φ: B → A is a finite extension of rings, B is an integrally closed domain, and A is an integral domain. Given nested primes q ⊂ q′ in B and a prime p′ of A lying over q′, there exists a prime p of A contained in p′ lying over q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric picture: extend chains of primes. Hypothesis 'integrally closed' on B is essential (counterexamples exist). Proof uses normal closure of K(A)/K(B), integral closure C of B in that normal extension, Lying Over and Going-Up in C, and an automorphism argument (Lemma 11.2.15) to move primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime avoidance (Proposition 11.2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If I and p_i (i∈I) are ideals and prime ideals of a ring A, and I ⊂ ⋃_{i=1}^n p_i, then I ⊂ p_i for some i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually proved by induction on n. Geometric interpretation: an ideal cannot be covered by finitely many proper closed subsets unless contained in one. Useful as a technical tool throughout proofs (e.g., Nagata's trick, Hartogs proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitively acting automorphisms on primes in integral closure (Lemma 11.2.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is an integrally closed domain, L/K(B) is a finite normal field extension, and C is the integral closure of B in L, then automorphisms of L over K(B) act transitively on primes of C lying over a given prime q′ of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the proof of the Going-Down Theorem: conjugates of a chosen prime in C allow producing a prime in A lying over a smaller prime. Standard number-theory-style argument with norms and prime avoidance to get a contradiction if transitivity failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension preserved under field extension for finite type k-schemes (Exercise 11.2.I)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a finite type k-scheme of pure dimension n and K/k is any field extension, then X_K has pure dimension n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to affine, then integral domain case. Write K/k as algebraic extension of a purely transcendental extension and use behavior of transcendence bases to show transcendence degree unchanged. Conceptual use: dimension of a scheme given by equations over Q doesn't change when considered over C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem (geometric and algebraic versions, 11.3.2 and 11.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric: If X is a locally Noetherian scheme and f a function, the irreducible components of V(f) have codimension 0 or 1. Algebraic: If A is Noetherian and f ∈ A, then every prime minimal among those containing f has codimension ≤ 1; if f is not a zero divisor, minimal primes containing f have codimension exactly 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the linear algebra fact that one equation cuts codimension 0 or 1. Useful consequences: locally principal closed subschemes have components of codimension 0 or 1; effective Cartier divisors are pure codimension 1. Full proofs are technical (see §11.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: UFD characterization via codimension-1 primes (Proposition 11.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian integral domain A, A is a unique factorization domain iff all codimension-1 prime ideals are principal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem and exercises: generators of codimension-1 primes are irreducible, Noetherian hypothesis ensures existence of factorization, uniqueness follows from prime components of V(f). Remarks point out the statement remains true without Noetherian hypothesis with more work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krull's Height Theorem (11.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X = Spec A with A Noetherian, and Z is an irreducible component of V(r1,...,r_ℓ) where r1,...,r_ℓ ∈ A. Then codimension(Z) ≤ ℓ (height ≤ number of generators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalization of Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem is more subtle than simple induction; full proof in §11.5. Interprets 'height' as codimension. Exercise 11.3.J asks to prove this in finitely generated domain (variety) case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic Hartogs's Lemma for Noetherian normal schemes (11.3.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a Noetherian normal integral domain, then A = ⋂_{p codimension 1} A_p (equality inside K(A)). Equivalently, a rational function with no poles at codimension-1 points is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: Noetherian normal schemes have the Hartogs property. The proof uses the ideal of denominators of a rational function, prime avoidance, localization at a minimal prime of that ideal, and integrality arguments. Generalizations: integral closure equals intersection of valuation rings containing A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypersurfaces meet projective varieties of dimension ≥1 (Exercise 11.3.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If X ⊂ P^n_k has dimension ≥1 and H is a nonempty hypersurface, then H meets X. (b) For X closed of dimension r, any codimension-r linear space meets X. (c) There is an intersection of r+1 nonempty hypersurfaces missing X. (d) Over infinite fields: there is an intersection of r hyperplanes meeting X in finitely many points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: use affine cones and Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem; for (c) construct hypersurfaces of sufficiently high degree avoiding generic points by induction; for (d) use density of choices over infinite fields. These are geometric intersection principles used repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invertibility criterion via codimension (Exercise 11.3.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Noetherian ring A, if f ∈ A is contained in no prime of codimension 0 or 1, then f is invertible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: a function vanishing nowhere is invertible (Exercise 4.3.G(b)). Use Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem to argue about minimal primes. Useful in proofs that relate vanishing loci to units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems of parameters and finite dimension of Noetherian local rings (Exercise 11.3.K)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Noetherian local rings have finite dimension: if V(g1,...,g_ℓ) = {[m]} then dim A ≤ ℓ. (b) Let d = dim A. There exist g1,...,g_d ∈ A such that V(g1,...,g_d) = {[m]}; these elements are a system of parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Krull's Height Theorem and prime avoidance to find elements that cut dimension down by 1 at each step. Geometric translation: a d-dimensional germ can be set-theoretically cut out by d equations, and one always needs at least d equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathology warning: codimension can behave oddly (example in §11.3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist Noetherian domains where a codimension-1 prime is a maximal (dimension 0) ideal: e.g., A = k[x]_{(x)}[t] with (xt−1) a maximal prime of codimension 1 while A has dimension ≥2, exhibiting that codimension and dimension can behave counterintuitively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric picture: V(xt−1) doesn't meet V(x) so it has no specializations there; shows necessity of hypotheses in various theorems and cautions when interpreting codimension in non-catenary situations.
